data.hypothesis: The best measured role candidate uses a guarded omp simd loop but makes no alignment claim; the scalar pointer formulation was much slower. This experiment checks whether a runtime-verified 16-byte aligned SIMD body helps: it peels up to three x cells after checking that input, velocity, and output line starts share a residue, and otherwise retains the unaligned SIMD path. The dynamic check and peel account for the interior and row offsets without assuming allocation alignment or an ISA.

memory_lessons.applicability: Compare single-timestep x-line variants under this frozen build; retain runtime correctness checks for all sizes and offsets.
memory_lessons.claim: The scalar pointer-traversal candidate measured 0.4530 s, while the row-local guarded omp simd candidate measured 0.0799 s and the indexed guarded omp simd candidate measured 0.0834 s. These results make SIMD exposure a relevant factor to test, but do not establish that alignment peeling will improve performance.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this runtime-aligned, peeled loop against the selected row-local SIMD parent under the official protocol.

data.notes: Uses selected parent 90846974b5f244eb as the base, with no imported source ideas. The aligned clause is used only after checking actual line-pointer residues and peeling the interior offset; fallback retains unaligned SIMD. Arithmetic order, spatial bounds, timestep parity, interface, and threading behavior are unchanged. No correctness run or performance measurement was performed here; the controller must validate and measure this candidate.
transformations: Check each row's actual input, velocity, and output pointer residues before claiming 16-byte alignment.
When residues match and the row is long enough, scalar-peel to an aligned starting point and apply guarded OpenMP SIMD to the remainder.
If the pointers do not share a residue, retain the unaligned guarded SIMD loop; preserve arithmetic ordering and bounds.
